## When Is Salary Sacrifice Not Worth It? Understanding Your Hourly to Annual Conversion

If you're paid by the hour or considering a salary offer, converting your hourly rate to an annual figure is a straightforward calculation. However, the real picture involves tax, superannuation, and decisions like salary sacrifice. Knowing when salary sacrifice is not worth it can save you money and help you plan your finances.

### The Basic Conversion Formula

To estimate your annual gross pay, multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role based on 38 hours per week, the formula is:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, if your hourly rate is $30, your annual gross would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This assumes you work every week at the same rate, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It also ignores salary sacrifice arrangements.

If you work part-time or casual, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. Casual employees typically receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate, so their effective hourly rate is higher. For instance, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for permanent employees, but casuals get $33.05 per hour including the loading. Remember, you should not type a rate that already includes casual loading into our [the timesheet](/) – instead, use the base rate and check the casual loading box.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many employers pay fortnightly. Your gross fortnightly pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. Using the example above, weekly pay is $30 × 38 = $1,140, so fortnightly gross is $2,280. This helps with budgeting and comparing to salary offers that are quoted annually.

### Distinguishing Minimum Wage, Award Rates, and Casual Loading

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage each year. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, or $1,004.90 per week. However, most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that may set higher minimum rates. Award rates vary by industry and occupation. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award.

Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base award or minimum wage rate. This compensates for not receiving paid leave. The loading is paid on top of the hourly rate, not included in it. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how to calculate it.

### Tax and Medicare

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies a progressive tax scale for residents in 2026–27:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. There are reductions for low-income earners, but the thresholds for 2026–27 were not confirmed at the time of this estimate, so we use the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds. This is an estimate only. For a more detailed breakdown of your take-home pay, see our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page.

### Superannuation Guarantee

Employers must pay superannuation on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% from 1 July 2026, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional cost to your employer. For example, if your annual ordinary earnings are $60,000, your employer contributes $7,200 to your super fund. This is separate from your take-home pay.

### When Is Salary Sacrifice Not Worth It?

Salary sacrifice involves arranging with your employer to reduce your pre-tax salary in exchange for benefits like extra super contributions, a car, or other fringe benefits. It can lower your taxable income, but it's not always beneficial.

Salary sacrifice is generally not worth it when:

- **Your marginal tax rate is low.** If you earn less than $18,200, you pay no tax, so sacrificing salary only reduces your cash flow without any tax saving.
- **You need immediate cash flow.** Sacrificing salary reduces your take-home pay. If you have high living expenses or debt, the short-term loss may outweigh the long-term super benefit.
- **You are close to the super contribution cap.** The concessional contributions cap for 2026–27 is $30,000 (including employer contributions). If your employer's super guarantee plus your salary sacrifice exceed this cap, you may pay extra tax.
- **Your employer does not pass on the FBT savings.** Some salary sacrifice arrangements, like cars, involve fringe benefits tax (FBT). If your employer does not share the FBT savings, you might be worse off.

Before entering a salary sacrifice arrangement, use our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page to understand the implications. Also consider your overall financial situation. For many workers on average earnings, salary sacrifice into super can be beneficial, but it's not a one-size-fits-all decision.

### State Differences in Ordinary-Time Earnings

The Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) data. In May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings averaged $2,083.70 per week nationally. However, these averages vary by state and territory due to industry mix, cost of living, and enterprise agreements. For example, mining-heavy states like Western Australia often have higher average earnings than Tasmania. Our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page provides more detail.

These state differences affect your conversion from hourly to annual. If you are negotiating a salary or hourly rate, consider where you work. A rate that is competitive in one state may be below average in another. Remember, the AWE figures are averages, not medians for your specific job. Use our [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page to research industry-specific rates.

### Putting It All Together

To estimate your annual pay, start with your hourly rate and multiply by your weekly hours and 52. Then subtract tax and Medicare to get an approximate take-home amount. Add super as a separate benefit. Consider whether salary sacrifice makes sense for you. And always check the relevant award or agreement for your minimum entitlements.

Our [the timesheet](/) calculator lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading. It provides an annual estimate, including tax and super, based on the assumptions above. Remember, this is an estimate – your actual pay may differ due to overtime, penalties, allowances, or salary packaging.

By understanding when salary sacrifice is not worth it, you can make informed decisions about your pay and benefits. Whether you are a full-time employee, casual, or contractor, the conversion from hourly to annual is a useful tool for financial planning.
